concepts.def: A chemical bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons, each atom contributing one electron to the shared pair. Covalent bonds are strong, so the carbon skeletons of biological molecules are stable; they hold the atoms of a single molecule together, in contrast to the weaker intermolecular attractions such as hydrogen bonds.

A carbon atom has four electrons in its outer shell and forms up to four covalent bonds, either as four single bonds or as a combination of single and double bonds, with other carbon atoms or with atoms of other non-metallic elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus. Because carbon–carbon bonds can be repeated indefinitely, carbon compounds can be unbranched chains (fatty acids), branched chains (amylopectin, glycogen), single rings (glucose, ribose) or multiple rings (steroids, the purine bases adenine and guanine), which is the basis of the diversity of the compounds on which life depends.

Prefixes attached to SI units to show a multiple or fraction of the unit: kilo (10³), centi (10⁻²), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶) and nano (10⁻⁹). Their meanings are not facts discovered about nature but conventions fixed by international agreement, so that a measurement such as 7 µm has the same meaning to every scientist regardless of language or country (a nature-of-science point).

A monomer is a small molecule that can be linked to others of the same kind; a polymer is a large molecule made of many monomers joined by covalent bonds; a macromolecule is any very large molecule. Polysaccharides, polypeptides and nucleic acids are polymers, and therefore macromolecules. Lipids such as triglycerides are large but are not polymers, because they are built from a fixed small number of different components rather than from a repeating monomer.

A reaction in which two molecules are joined by a covalent bond with the release of a water molecule, formed from an -OH group of one molecule and an -H from the other. Monomers are linked into polymers by repeated condensation reactions, each forming one bond and releasing one water molecule, so joining n monomers into a chain releases n − 1 water molecules. Condensation reactions in cells are catalysed by enzymes.

The three classes of biological polymer produced by condensation. Polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) are polymers of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds; polypeptides are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds; nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polymers of nucleotides linked by covalent bonds between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next.

A reaction in which a covalent bond between two parts of a molecule is broken by the addition of water: the water molecule is split, and the -H is added to one product and the -OH to the other, which is why the reaction is named hydrolysis ("splitting with water"). Digestion breaks polymers into monomers by enzyme-catalysed hydrolysis, so hydrolysing a chain of n monomers uses n − 1 water molecules. Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation.

A single sugar unit, the monomer of polysaccharides. Monosaccharides are classified by the number of carbon atoms they contain: a pentose has five (ribose and deoxyribose) and a hexose has six (glucose, fructose and galactose). In molecular diagrams they are usually drawn in ring form, in which one oxygen atom forms part of the ring and one or more carbon atoms lie outside it, so the class is found by counting all the carbon atoms, in and outside the ring, not by counting the atoms that make up the ring.

concepts.term: Properties of glucose in relation to its use
concepts.def: Glucose (a hexose) is the main respiratory substrate and transport sugar in many organisms because of four properties: it is soluble in water, since its polar hydroxyl (-OH) groups form hydrogen bonds with water; it is therefore transportable, dissolved in blood plasma or other fluids; it is chemically stable, so it does not break down during transport or storage unless enzymes act on it; and its oxidation in cell respiration to carbon dioxide and water yields a large amount of energy.

The energy storage polysaccharide of plants, a polymer of alpha-glucose made of amylose (unbranched chains that coil into a helix) and amylopectin (chains with occasional branches). Coiling and branching make starch compact, so much glucose is stored in a small volume; its large molecular size makes it relatively insoluble, so it has no osmotic effect on the cell; and alpha-glucose monomers can be added by condensation or removed by hydrolysis at chain ends with relative ease, so the store can be built up or mobilized as needed.

The energy storage polysaccharide of animals (and fungi), a polymer of alpha-glucose similar to amylopectin but more frequently branched. Its branching makes it compact and provides many chain ends at which glucose can be added by condensation or removed by hydrolysis at the same time, allowing rapid mobilization; its large size makes it relatively insoluble, so glycogen granules in liver and muscle cells do not disturb the cell's osmotic balance.

Two forms (isomers) of glucose with the same molecular formula, C₆H₁₂O₆, that differ only in the orientation of the hydroxyl group on carbon atom 1 in the ring form: below the plane of the ring in alpha-glucose and above it in beta-glucose. Starch and glycogen are polymers of alpha-glucose; cellulose is a polymer of beta-glucose, and this small difference determines whether the polymer coils and branches or forms straight chains.

The structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls, an unbranched polymer of beta-glucose. Because of the orientation of the hydroxyl group on carbon 1 of beta-glucose, each successive monomer is rotated 180° relative to its neighbours, so the chain is straight rather than coiled. Straight chains lie side by side and are grouped into bundles (microfibrils) cross-linked by many hydrogen bonds between chains, giving cellulose the high tensile strength that lets the cell wall resist the pressure of the cell contents.

A protein with one or more carbohydrate chains covalently attached. Glycoproteins in the plasma membrane have their carbohydrate part projecting outwards from the cell surface, where the particular sequence of sugars acts as a marker that other cells and the immune system can recognize, so glycoproteins are the basis of cell–cell recognition, including the recognition of cells as belonging to the organism itself.

Glycoproteins (and glycolipids) on the surface of red blood cells whose carbohydrate chains determine a person's ABO blood group. The A antigen and the B antigen share the same base chain and differ only in the monosaccharide added at its end, by an enzyme encoded by the person's ABO alleles. Group A cells carry the A antigen, group B cells the B antigen, group AB cells both; group O cells carry the unmodified base chain and neither the A nor the B antigen, so there is no separate "O antigen". Recognition of these antigens by antibodies is why transfused blood must be matched.

A substance in living organisms that dissolves in non-polar solvents but is only sparingly soluble in aqueous (water-based) solvents. Lipids are defined by this solubility rather than by a single structure, and include fats (triglycerides that are solid at about 20°C), oils (triglycerides that are liquid at that temperature), waxes and steroids.

Describes a molecule or region of a molecule that does not dissolve in or associate with water. Lipids are hydrophobic because they consist mostly of carbon and hydrogen atoms joined by non-polar covalent bonds, with few or no polar groups able to form hydrogen bonds with water; water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and the non-polar molecules are excluded, so they cluster together. Lipids are not insoluble because they are large: a triglyceride is far smaller than a soluble protein.

A lipid formed when one glycerol molecule is linked by condensation reactions to three fatty acid molecules. Each of the three hydroxyl groups of glycerol reacts with the carboxyl group of a fatty acid to form an ester bond and release a water molecule, so three water molecules are released in total. Fats and oils are triglycerides. A triglyceride is not a polymer, because it is made from a fixed number of components rather than a chain of repeating monomers.

A lipid formed by condensation reactions in which one glycerol molecule is linked to two fatty acid molecules and one phosphate group. The two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic and the phosphate head is hydrophilic, so the molecule is amphipathic and forms the bilayers of cell membranes.

concepts.term: Saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids
concepts.def: Fatty acids are classified by the number of carbon–carbon double bonds (C=C) in their hydrocarbon chain: a saturated fatty acid has none (every carbon carries as many hydrogen atoms as it can), a monounsaturated fatty acid has one and a polyunsaturated fatty acid has two or more. The C=O double bond of the carboxyl group is present in every fatty acid and does not count towards unsaturation.

concepts.term: Effect of C=C double bonds on melting point
concepts.def: Each C=C double bond puts a kink in the hydrocarbon chain of a fatty acid, so molecules of unsaturated fatty acids and the triglycerides made from them cannot pack closely together; the intermolecular attractions between them are weaker and the melting point is lower. Saturated chains are straight, pack closely and melt at higher temperatures. Plants, which are at environmental temperature, store energy as oils rich in unsaturated fatty acids that remain liquid when it is cool; endotherms, which maintain a high, constant body temperature, store fats with a higher proportion of saturated fatty acids, which are solid at room temperature but sufficiently fluid at body temperature.

Triglycerides stored in adipose tissue suit long-term energy storage because they release about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates when oxidized, they are insoluble so they can be stored in large amounts without osmotic effects and without the water that accompanies glycogen, and they are chemically stable. Glycogen is used for shorter-term storage from which glucose can be mobilized quickly.

Adipose tissue beneath the skin is a poor conductor of heat, so it slows the loss of heat from the body to the surroundings. It is valuable to endotherms, which maintain a body temperature above that of their habitat: the colder the habitat relative to body temperature, the thicker the layer that is useful, as in the blubber of seals and whales in polar seas. The insulating layer is not the source of the heat it retains, which comes from the animal's metabolism, and it is of little use for retaining heat in ectotherms, whose body temperature is close to that of their surroundings.

Describes a molecule that has both a hydrophilic (water-attracting) region and a hydrophobic (water-excluded) region. A phospholipid is amphipathic: its phosphate head is hydrophilic and its two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic. The term does not mean that the molecule is both an acid and a base.

The double layer of phospholipids that forms the basis of all cell membranes. In water, amphipathic phospholipids spontaneously arrange themselves so that the hydrophilic heads face the water on both surfaces and the hydrophobic tails face inwards, away from water, forming the interior of the bilayer. The arrangement forms and is maintained because the tails are excluded from water, not because phospholipids are covalently bonded to one another, so the bilayer is stable yet fluid.

A lipid whose molecules are built on four fused rings of carbon atoms, three six-membered and one five-membered, which is how a steroid is recognized in a molecular diagram. Steroids are non-polar (hydrophobic), so they can pass through the hydrophobic interior of a phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion and reach receptors inside cells.

Steroid hormones, both built on the four fused carbon rings that characterize steroids: oestradiol is the main oestrogen and testosterone the main androgen. Being non-polar steroids, they diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer of their target cells and bind to receptors inside the cell, unlike protein hormones, which cannot cross the bilayer.

mcqs.q: Carbon forms an enormous diversity of compounds, on which life is based. Which statement about the bonding of a single carbon atom is correct?
options: It forms up to four covalent bonds, single or double, with carbon or other non-metal atoms
It forms any number of covalent bonds, which is why so many carbon compounds exist
It transfers its four outer electrons to other atoms, giving charged compounds
It links to neighbouring carbon atoms by weak hydrogen bonds that are easily broken
mcqs.specStatementText: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
mcqs.explain: A carbon atom has four outer electrons, so it can form up to four covalent bonds, as four single bonds or a combination of single and double bonds, with other carbon atoms or with atoms of other non-metallic elements. Repeating this gives chains, branches and rings.
rationales: A carbon atom has four outer electrons, so it can form up to four covalent bonds, as four single bonds or a combination of single and double bonds, with other carbon atoms or with atoms of other non-metallic elements. Repeating this gives chains, branches and rings.

A student who merges "carbon forms many bonds" with "carbon forms many compounds" picks this. The maximum is four bonds per atom; the diversity comes from carbon atoms linking to each other repeatedly in chains and rings.
A student who models every bond on ionic bonding picks this. Carbon forms covalent bonds, sharing a pair of electrons with each partner atom, so its compounds are uncharged molecules.

A student who thinks of hydrogen bonds as the general bond of biology picks this. Carbon atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds; hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between molecules or parts of molecules.

mcqs.q: A student measures the diameter of a cell as 7 µm. What is this diameter in nanometres?
options: 70 nm, because each prefix is ten times the next
7000 nm, because one micrometre is 1000 nanometres
0.007 nm, because a smaller unit means a smaller number
7 000 000 nm, because a micrometre is 10⁻³ of a metre
mcqs.specStatementText: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
mcqs.explain: 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m and 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, so 1 µm = 1000 nm. The length is unchanged; it is expressed in a smaller unit, so the number is larger: 7 × 1000 = 7000 nm.
rationales: A student who treats each SI prefix as a factor of ten picks this. Micro is 10⁻⁶ and nano is 10⁻⁹, so the two differ by a factor of 1000, not 10.
1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m and 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, so 1 µm = 1000 nm. The length is unchanged; it is expressed in a smaller unit, so the number is larger: 7 × 1000 = 7000 nm.
A student who divides because "nano is smaller" picks this. A smaller unit fits into the same length more times, so converting micrometres to nanometres multiplies by 1000.
A student who has swapped milli and micro picks this, treating 7 µm as 7 × 10⁻³ m. Micro is 10⁻⁶, so 7 µm is 7 × 10⁻⁶ m, which is 7000 nm.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the SI prefixes kilo, centi, milli, micro and nano is correct?
options: Their meanings were discovered by scientists measuring natural objects
Each prefix is one tenth of the prefix that comes before it
Their meanings are conventions fixed by international agreement
"micro" means one thousandth, and "milli" means one millionth
mcqs.specStatementText: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
mcqs.explain: The values of the SI prefixes are scientific conventions agreed internationally so that a measurement means the same thing to every scientist. They are agreed, not discovered, which is a nature-of-science point the guide makes explicitly.
rationales: A student who treats every part of science as discovered fact picks this. The prefixes are conventions that could have been defined differently; what is discovered is the size of the objects measured with them.
A student who generalizes from centi and milli, which really are a factor of ten apart, picks this. Milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶) and nano (10⁻⁹) are each a factor of 1000 apart.

The values of the SI prefixes are scientific conventions agreed internationally so that a measurement means the same thing to every scientist. They are agreed, not discovered, which is a nature-of-science point the guide makes explicitly.
A student who has the two m-prefixes swapped picks this. Milli is one thousandth (10⁻³) and micro is one millionth (10⁻⁶); that is why cells are measured in micrometres.

mcqs.q: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide. What happens in this reaction?
options: A molecule of water is taken in and split to supply the atoms that join the monomers
A hydrogen bond forms between the two monomers, holding them together as a disaccharide
Water dissolves the two monomers so that they meet, but no water is formed or used
A covalent bond forms between the monomers and a molecule of water is released
mcqs.specStatementText: Condensation joins monomers into polymers
mcqs.explain: In a condensation reaction an -OH from one monomer and an -H from the other are removed and combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers. Repeated condensations build a polysaccharide.
rationales: A student who has the two reactions swapped picks this. Water is used and split in hydrolysis, which breaks bonds; condensation forms a bond and releases water.
A student who thinks of hydrogen bonds as the bond of biology picks this. The bond formed by condensation is a strong covalent bond, which is why the disaccharide is stable until it is hydrolysed.
A student who sees water only as the solvent picks this. Water is a product of condensation: one molecule is released for every bond formed.

In a condensation reaction an -OH from one monomer and an -H from the other are removed and combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers. Repeated condensations build a polysaccharide.

mcqs.q: A polypeptide made of 100 amino acids is completely hydrolysed into free amino acids. How many water molecules are used in the process?
options: 99 water molecules
100 water molecules
1 water molecule
0 water molecules
mcqs.specStatementText: Hydrolysis splits polymers back into monomers
mcqs.explain: A chain of 100 amino acids contains 99 peptide bonds. Each hydrolysis reaction breaks one bond and uses one water molecule, which is split to supply the -H and -OH added to the products, so 99 water molecules are used.
rationales: A chain of 100 amino acids contains 99 peptide bonds. Each hydrolysis reaction breaks one bond and uses one water molecule, which is split to supply the -H and -OH added to the products, so 99 water molecules are used.
A student who counts one bond per monomer picks this. Bonds lie between monomers, so 100 monomers are joined by 99 bonds, and hydrolysing them uses 99 water molecules.
A student who reads "polymer + water → monomers" as a single reaction picks this. Each bond needs its own hydrolysis reaction and its own water molecule.
A student who thinks water is merely the solvent picks this. Water is a reactant in hydrolysis: one molecule is consumed and split for every bond broken.

mcqs.q: Why is the digestion of a polymer into its monomers described as a hydrolysis reaction?
options: Water acts only as the solvent in which enzymes break the polymer into its monomers
Water molecules are split, and the -H and -OH produced are added to the monomers
Breaking the bonds between the monomers releases the energy that was stored in those bonds
Water molecules are released as each bond between neighbouring monomers is broken
mcqs.specStatementText: Hydrolysis splits polymers back into monomers
mcqs.explain: Hydrolysis means splitting with water. For each bond broken, one water molecule is split; its -H is added to one product and its -OH to the other, so the water is incorporated into the monomers.
rationales: A student who sees water as the inert medium picks this. Water is a reactant that is split and incorporated into the products, which is exactly what the name hydrolysis records.
Hydrolysis means splitting with water. For each bond broken, one water molecule is split; its -H is added to one product and its -OH to the other, so the water is incorporated into the monomers.
A student who believes bond-breaking releases energy picks this. Hydrolysis releases very little energy; the energy from food is released later, when monomers are oxidized in cell respiration.
A student who has swapped the two reactions picks this. Water is released in condensation, when bonds form; in hydrolysis water is used up as bonds break.

mcqs.q: Two monosaccharides, P and Q, are drawn in their ring forms. In P the ring is made of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, with one further carbon atom (in a CH₂OH group) attached outside the ring. In Q the ring is also made of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, but two further carbon atoms (each in a CH₂OH group) are attached outside the ring. How should P and Q be classified?
options: Both P and Q are pentose sugars
Both P and Q are hexose sugars
P is a pentose and Q is a hexose
P and Q are alpha and beta glucose
mcqs.specStatementText: Monosaccharides, and why glucose suits its job
mcqs.explain: Pentoses and hexoses are named for their total number of carbon atoms. P has 4 + 1 = 5 carbon atoms, so it is a pentose (such as ribose); Q has 4 + 2 = 6 carbon atoms, so it is a hexose (such as fructose), even though its ring has only five atoms.
rationales: A student who counts the atoms in the ring picks this: both rings have five atoms. But one ring atom is oxygen and carbon atoms also lie outside the ring, so the ring size does not give the number of carbons.
A student who assumes every monosaccharide has six carbons, like glucose, picks this. P has only five carbon atoms in total, so it is a pentose.

Pentoses and hexoses are named for their total number of carbon atoms. P has 4 + 1 = 5 carbon atoms, so it is a pentose (such as ribose); Q has 4 + 2 = 6 carbon atoms, so it is a hexose (such as fructose), even though its ring has only five atoms.

A student who thinks any two differently drawn ring sugars are the alpha and beta forms picks this. Alpha- and beta-glucose have the same atoms and differ only in the orientation of one -OH group; P and Q differ in their number of carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly links a property of glucose to the way it is used in organisms?
options: Glucose breaks down readily on its own, which is why it is used as a respiratory substrate
Glucose dissolves in water because its molecules are small, so it is easily transported
Glucose is highly soluble, so cells store large quantities of it dissolved in their cytoplasm
Glucose is chemically stable, so it is transported in blood plasma without breaking down
mcqs.specStatementText: Monosaccharides, and why glucose suits its job
mcqs.explain: Glucose does not break down spontaneously; its covalent bonds are broken only when enzymes act on it in cell respiration. This stability, together with its solubility, is what allows it to be carried in the blood to the cells that oxidize it.
rationales: A student who equates energy-rich with unstable picks this. Glucose is chemically stable; its energy is released only by controlled, enzyme-catalysed oxidation in cell respiration.

A student who uses size as the rule for solubility picks this. Glucose dissolves because its polar hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water; small non-polar molecules such as steroids do not dissolve.

A student who does not consider osmotic effects picks this. Cells convert glucose into relatively insoluble polysaccharides for storage; a high concentration of dissolved glucose would draw in water by osmosis.

Glucose does not break down spontaneously; its covalent bonds are broken only when enzymes act on it in cell respiration. This stability, together with its solubility, is what allows it to be carried in the blood to the cells that oxidize it.

mcqs.q: Liver cells store glucose in the form of glycogen. Why is the glucose not simply stored as free glucose?
options: Glycogen is relatively insoluble because of its size, so it does not affect the osmotic balance of the cell
Glycogen is insoluble because it is non-polar, so it stays separate from the watery cytoplasm
The branches of glycogen make its glucose hard to remove, so the store is not used up too quickly
Glycogen stores extra energy in the glycosidic bonds that link its glucose monomers together
mcqs.specStatementText: Starch and glycogen store energy compactly
mcqs.explain: Glycogen is a very large molecule and is relatively insoluble, so large amounts can be stored without raising the solute concentration of the cytoplasm. Free glucose is soluble and would draw water into the cell by osmosis.
rationales: Glycogen is a very large molecule and is relatively insoluble, so large amounts can be stored without raising the solute concentration of the cytoplasm. Free glucose is soluble and would draw water into the cell by osmosis.
A student who reuses the lipid explanation for insolubility picks this. Glycogen is covered in polar hydroxyl groups; it is relatively insoluble only because its molecules are so large.
A student who imagines branches as protection picks this. Branching does the opposite: it provides many chain ends at which glucose can be removed rapidly by hydrolysis.

A student who believes energy is stored in bonds picks this. Polymerizing glucose does not add energy; the energy is released when glucose is oxidized in cell respiration, and glycogen is simply a compact, osmotically inert way of holding it.

mcqs.q: In glycogen a branch occurs roughly every 10 glucose monomers; in the amylopectin of starch a branch occurs roughly every 25 monomers, and amylose is unbranched. Animals often need to release glucose from their stores very rapidly. Which explanation best accounts for the high degree of branching in glycogen?
options: Branches shield the glycosidic bonds, slowing hydrolysis so that the store is released steadily over time
Monomers are removed by hydrolysis at chain ends, so more branches give more ends to act on at once
Branching makes glycogen non-polar, so that it remains insoluble until the glucose is actually required
Each branch point adds a bond in which extra energy is stored for release when the bond is broken
mcqs.specStatementText: Starch and glycogen store energy compactly
mcqs.explain: Glucose is removed from a polysaccharide only at the ends of chains. Every branch point creates an extra end, so a molecule with a branch every 10 monomers can be hydrolysed at many more points simultaneously than amylopectin, matching an animal's need for rapid mobilization.
rationales: A student who sees branches as protection picks this. Branches expose more chain ends, speeding hydrolysis; a store that was released slowly would not suit an animal needing glucose quickly.

Glucose is removed from a polysaccharide only at the ends of chains. Every branch point creates an extra end, so a molecule with a branch every 10 monomers can be hydrolysed at many more points simultaneously than amylopectin, matching an animal's need for rapid mobilization.

A student who explains insolubility by non-polarity picks this. Glycogen is a polar molecule covered in hydroxyl groups; it is relatively insoluble because of its size, and branching has nothing to do with polarity.

A student who believes bonds store energy picks this. Breaking glycosidic bonds absorbs a little energy rather than releasing it; the energy comes from oxidizing the glucose released, however many branches there are.

mcqs.q: Amylose, a polymer of alpha-glucose, forms a coiled chain, whereas cellulose, a polymer of beta-glucose, forms a straight chain. Why does the cellulose chain not coil?
options: Beta-glucose has a different molecular formula, and its extra atoms make the chain rigid
Covalent bonds between neighbouring cellulose chains pull each chain out straight and flat
Each beta-glucose is rotated 180° relative to its neighbours, so the chain is straight
Branches along the cellulose chain, as in amylopectin, prevent the chain from coiling
mcqs.specStatementText: Cellulose: straight chains bundled into a strong wall
mcqs.explain: In beta-glucose the -OH on carbon 1 points above the ring, so successive monomers must alternate in orientation (each rotated 180°) to form the glycosidic bond. The alternating orientation cancels any tendency to curve, giving straight chains that can be bundled and cross-linked by hydrogen bonds.
rationales: A student who believes alpha- and beta-glucose are different sugars picks this. Both are C₆H₁₂O₆; they differ only in the orientation of one -OH group, and that alone produces the alternating, straight chain.

A student who expects covalent cross-links picks this. Neighbouring chains are linked only by hydrogen bonds, and the straightness of each chain comes from the alternating orientation of its own monomers.

In beta-glucose the -OH on carbon 1 points above the ring, so successive monomers must alternate in orientation (each rotated 180°) to form the glycosidic bond. The alternating orientation cancels any tendency to curve, giving straight chains that can be bundled and cross-linked by hydrogen bonds.
A student who transfers the structure of starch to cellulose picks this. Cellulose chains are unbranched; they are straight because of the alternating orientation of beta-glucose monomers.

mcqs.q: Cellulose gives plant cell walls high tensile strength. Which feature of cellulose is responsible for this?
options: The glycosidic bonds within cellulose are very much stronger than those within starch
The chains coil into tight helices that stretch and recoil like a spring
Beta-glucose is a larger monomer than alpha-glucose, giving thicker chains
Straight chains lie side by side in bundles, cross-linked by many hydrogen bonds
mcqs.specStatementText: Cellulose: straight chains bundled into a strong wall
mcqs.explain: The straight, unbranched chains of beta-glucose pack side by side and are grouped into bundles in which a very large number of hydrogen bonds link the chains. Although each hydrogen bond is weak, together they give the bundles great resistance to stretching.
rationales: A student who looks for strength in stronger covalent bonds picks this. The glycosidic bonds in cellulose and starch are both covalent and of similar strength; the difference lies in how the chains are arranged and cross-linked.
A student who transfers the coiled shape of amylose to cellulose picks this. Cellulose chains are straight, and it is their side-by-side bundling, not coiling, that gives strength.
A student who thinks the two forms of glucose differ in size or atoms picks this. Alpha- and beta-glucose have identical formulae; beta-glucose differs only in the orientation of the -OH on carbon 1.

The straight, unbranched chains of beta-glucose pack side by side and are grouped into bundles in which a very large number of hydrogen bonds link the chains. Although each hydrogen bond is weak, together they give the bundles great resistance to stretching.

mcqs.q: The ABO blood groups depend on glycoproteins on the surface of red blood cells. Which statement about these ABO antigens is correct?
options: The A and B antigens differ only in the sugar at the end of their carbohydrate chain
The A and B antigens are two entirely different proteins with unrelated amino acid sequences
Group O red blood cells carry a third antigen, the O antigen, in the place of the A or B
The carbohydrate part of each antigen projects inwards into the cell's cytoplasm
mcqs.specStatementText: Glycoproteins let cells recognize each other
mcqs.explain: ABO antigens are glycoproteins with a shared base carbohydrate chain. The alleles of the ABO gene encode enzymes that add different terminal monosaccharides to that chain, producing the A or the B antigen, and it is this small difference in the carbohydrate that other cells and antibodies recognize.
rationales: ABO antigens are glycoproteins with a shared base carbohydrate chain. The alleles of the ABO gene encode enzymes that add different terminal monosaccharides to that chain, producing the A or the B antigen, and it is this small difference in the carbohydrate that other cells and antibodies recognize.

A student who thinks of antigens only as proteins picks this. The identity of an ABO antigen lies in its carbohydrate chain, not its protein; A and B share the same base and differ in one terminal sugar.
A student who extends the A/B naming pattern to O picks this. Group O cells carry the unmodified base chain and neither the A nor the B antigen; there is no O antigen.

A student who has not registered the orientation of glycoproteins picks this. The carbohydrate faces outwards from the cell surface, which is what allows it to act in cell–cell recognition and to be met by antibodies.

mcqs.q: A triglyceride is only sparingly soluble in water but dissolves readily in a non-polar solvent. What explains this?
options: Its molecules are too large to fit between water molecules, but a non-polar solvent has more room
Its molecules are mostly non-polar C–H bonds, with few groups that hydrogen-bond to water
Its molecules are less dense than water, so they float on the surface rather than dissolving
It is a polymer of fatty acids, and polymers such as starch do not dissolve in water either
mcqs.specStatementText: Lipids are defined by what they dissolve in
mcqs.explain: Lipids are hydrophobic because they are non-polar. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and exclude molecules that cannot join in, so a triglyceride is sparingly soluble in water; in a non-polar solvent, whose molecules interact by the same weak attractions, it dissolves readily.
rationales: A student who reuses the size explanation for polysaccharides picks this. A triglyceride is far smaller than a soluble protein; its insolubility in water comes from its non-polar nature, not its size.

Lipids are hydrophobic because they are non-polar. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and exclude molecules that cannot join in, so a triglyceride is sparingly soluble in water; in a non-polar solvent, whose molecules interact by the same weak attractions, it dissolves readily.
A student who merges floating with not mixing picks this. Density decides whether a liquid floats, not whether it dissolves: ethanol is less dense than water yet mixes with it completely.

A student who classes triglycerides as polymers picks this. A triglyceride is one glycerol linked to three fatty acids, not a polymer, and its behaviour in solvents is explained by polarity, not by polymer size.

mcqs.q: Which components are linked together by condensation reactions to form one phospholipid molecule?
options: One glycerol, three fatty acids and one phosphate group
Three glycerol molecules, one fatty acid and one phosphate group
One glycerol, two fatty acids and one phosphate group
Many fatty acid monomers joined in a chain, plus one phosphate group
mcqs.specStatementText: Triglycerides and phospholipids are built by condensation
mcqs.explain: Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups. In a phospholipid two of them are linked by condensation to fatty acids and the third to a phosphate group, giving a molecule with two hydrophobic tails and a hydrophilic head.
rationales: A student who reads "phosphate added to a triglyceride" literally picks this. Glycerol can link only three components, so the phosphate replaces one fatty acid rather than being added to three.
A student who reads the tri- of triglyceride as three glycerols picks this pattern. Lipids built on glycerol have one glycerol; it is the number of fatty acids that varies.

Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups. In a phospholipid two of them are linked by condensation to fatty acids and the third to a phosphate group, giving a molecule with two hydrophobic tails and a hydrophilic head.
A student who assumes lipids are polymers picks this. A phospholipid is not a chain of monomers: it has a fixed structure of one glycerol, two fatty acids and one phosphate group.

mcqs.q: One glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules react by condensation to form one triglyceride. How much water is produced?
options: One water molecule is released
Four water molecules are released
No water is released; water is used up
Three water molecules are released
mcqs.specStatementText: Triglycerides and phospholipids are built by condensation
mcqs.explain: Each of the three hydroxyl groups of glycerol reacts with the carboxyl group of one fatty acid in a separate condensation reaction, forming an ester bond and releasing one water molecule, so three water molecules are released in total.
rationales: A student who imagines the whole molecule forming in a single reaction picks this. Three separate bonds form, and each condensation releases its own water molecule.
A student who counts one water molecule per component picks this. Water is released per bond formed, and four components are joined by three bonds.
A student who has swapped condensation and hydrolysis picks this. Condensation releases water as bonds form; it is hydrolysis, the reverse reaction, that uses water up.

Each of the three hydroxyl groups of glycerol reacts with the carboxyl group of one fatty acid in a separate condensation reaction, forming an ester bond and releasing one water molecule, so three water molecules are released in total.

mcqs.q: Three fatty acids each have 18 carbon atoms in their chain. X has no C=C double bonds, Y has one and Z has three. Which has the lowest melting point, and why?
options: Z, because its C=C bonds kink the chain so that molecules pack less closely together
X, because C=C bonds are stronger than single bonds and hold Y and Z molecules together
Z, because it has the fewest hydrogen atoms and so the fewest bonds to break as it melts
X, because having no double bonds makes it the unsaturated one, and unsaturated fats melt lowest
mcqs.specStatementText: Double bonds, melting point and where fats are stored
mcqs.explain: Each C=C double bond puts a kink in the hydrocarbon chain. The kinked molecules of Z cannot pack closely, so the intermolecular attractions between them are weakest and less energy is needed to separate them: Z, the polyunsaturated fatty acid, melts at the lowest temperature.
rationales: Each C=C double bond puts a kink in the hydrocarbon chain. The kinked molecules of Z cannot pack closely, so the intermolecular attractions between them are weakest and less energy is needed to separate them: Z, the polyunsaturated fatty acid, melts at the lowest temperature.

A student who confuses bonds within molecules with attractions between molecules picks this. C=C bonds are within each molecule; what matters for melting is how closely the molecules pack, and straight saturated chains such as X pack most closely and melt highest.

A student who counts the bonds to be broken picks this. Melting breaks no covalent bonds; it overcomes the weak attractions between molecules. Z does melt lowest, but only because its kinked chains pack least closely, not because it contains fewer bonds.

A student who takes "saturated" to mean full of double bonds picks this. A fatty acid is saturated with hydrogen, not with double bonds: X, with no C=C, is the saturated one, and its straight chains pack most closely, so it melts highest, not lowest.

mcqs.q: A student analysed two energy stores. Oil from a plant seed contained 12% saturated and 88% unsaturated fatty acids; fat from a mammal's adipose tissue contained 55% saturated and 45% unsaturated fatty acids. At 20°C the oil was liquid and the fat was solid. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?
options: The mammal's fat must be solid inside its body, so it requires the higher melting point that a high proportion of saturated fatty acids provides, whereas the seed's oil only needs to be liquid at room temperature

The mammal keeps a high, constant body temperature at which a store rich in saturated fatty acids stays fluid enough, while the seed is at lower environmental temperatures and needs unsaturated fatty acids with low melting points
The mammal's fat is solid because saturated fatty acids contain many C=C double bonds, which raise the melting point, whereas the unsaturated fatty acids of the oil have none and so remain liquid

The oil is liquid because its unsaturated fatty acids have fewer hydrogen atoms and so fewer covalent bonds to break when they melt, whereas the mammal's saturated fatty acids have more bonds to break and stay solid
mcqs.specStatementText: Double bonds, melting point and where fats are stored
mcqs.explain: Saturated fatty acids raise the melting point; unsaturated ones lower it. An endotherm maintains a body temperature well above 20°C, so a store with a high proportion of saturated fatty acids remains sufficiently fluid inside it. A plant is at environmental temperature, which is often low, so its store must be an oil rich in unsaturated fatty acids that stays liquid.
rationales: A student who judges the state of a stored fat at room temperature picks this. The relevant temperature is the mammal's body temperature, at which its fat is sufficiently fluid; being solid at 20°C says nothing about its state at 37°C.

Saturated fatty acids raise the melting point; unsaturated ones lower it. An endotherm maintains a body temperature well above 20°C, so a store with a high proportion of saturated fatty acids remains sufficiently fluid inside it. A plant is at environmental temperature, which is often low, so its store must be an oil rich in unsaturated fatty acids that stays liquid.

A student who thinks "saturated" means full of double bonds picks this. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C bonds and pack closely, which is why they raise the melting point; it is the unsaturated fatty acids that have C=C bonds.

A student who thinks melting breaks covalent bonds picks this. Melting leaves every molecule intact and only overcomes the attractions between molecules; the oil melts lower because the kinks from its C=C bonds stop the chains packing closely.

mcqs.q: Which property of triglycerides makes them well suited to long-term energy storage in adipose tissue?
options: They release less energy per gram than carbohydrates, so a store of them lasts longer
They are very large molecules, so they cannot dissolve and leave the adipose cell
They release about twice the energy per gram of carbohydrates when oxidized
Their many ester bonds store energy that is released when the bonds are broken
mcqs.specStatementText: Adipose tissue: energy store and insulator
mcqs.explain: Triglycerides yield roughly twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, and they are stored without the water that accompanies glycogen and without osmotic effects, so a great deal of energy is held in a small, stable mass, which is what a long-term store needs.
rationales: A student who thinks of carbohydrate as "the energy food" picks this. Triglycerides release about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates; a store lasts because it is large and compact, not because it is low in energy.

A student who explains lipid insolubility by size picks this. Triglycerides are insoluble because they are non-polar, not because they are large; a triglyceride is far smaller than a glycogen molecule.

Triglycerides yield roughly twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, and they are stored without the water that accompanies glycogen and without osmotic effects, so a great deal of energy is held in a small, stable mass, which is what a long-term store needs.

A student who believes energy is stored in bonds picks this. Breaking ester bonds by hydrolysis releases very little energy; the large yield comes from oxidizing the fatty acids and glycerol in cell respiration.

mcqs.q: A seal living in polar seas has a layer of adipose tissue (blubber) several centimetres thick beneath its skin. A dolphin of similar size living in tropical seas has a much thinner layer, and a cod living in the same polar seas as the seal has very little adipose tissue beneath its skin. Which explanation accounts for all three observations?
options: All animals in cold water need thick insulation, so the cod must have an equally thick layer of fat elsewhere in its body to keep itself warm in the polar sea
Blubber generates the heat that keeps the seal warm in polar water, the dolphin needs to generate less heat in warm water, and the cod does not generate any heat at all
Blubber traps a layer of air against the skin, the dolphin's warmer water means that less air is needed, and the cod's scales cannot hold a layer of air in place under water
Adipose tissue slows heat loss, so an endotherm needs more of it the larger the gap between its body and habitat temperatures, and the cod's body is at almost the temperature of the water
mcqs.specStatementText: Adipose tissue: energy store and insulator
mcqs.explain: Blubber is a poor conductor of heat, so it reduces the rate of heat loss from a warm body to colder surroundings. The seal maintains a body temperature far above that of polar water and needs thick insulation; the dolphin in warm water loses heat more slowly and needs less; the cod is an ectotherm at almost the temperature of the water, so insulation would retain no heat.
rationales: A student who links insulation to habitat alone picks this. The cod is an ectotherm with a body temperature close to the water's, so a fat layer could not keep it warm; only endotherms, whose bodies are warmer than their habitat, benefit from thick insulation.

A student who thinks fat produces warmth picks this. Blubber does not generate heat; it slows the loss of heat produced by metabolism. Its thickness reflects how much heat loss must be prevented, not how much heat must be made.

A student who transfers the trapped-air mechanism of fur and feathers picks this. Blubber contains no air; the triglyceride-filled tissue is itself a poor conductor, which is why it insulates under water where trapped air would be lost.

Blubber is a poor conductor of heat, so it reduces the rate of heat loss from a warm body to colder surroundings. The seal maintains a body temperature far above that of polar water and needs thick insulation; the dolphin in warm water loses heat more slowly and needs less; the cod is an ectotherm at almost the temperature of the water, so insulation would retain no heat.

mcqs.q: Phospholipids are shaken with water in a test tube, with no cells or enzymes present. What happens, and why?
options: Bilayers form, because the hydrophilic heads face the water and the hydrophobic tails face each other
Nothing organized forms, because phospholipid bilayers can only be built by enzymes inside living cells
Bilayers form, because covalent bonds link the fatty acid tails of neighbouring phospholipids
The phospholipids react with the water, because being amphipathic means acting as both an acid and a base
mcqs.specStatementText: Phospholipids arrange themselves into bilayers
mcqs.explain: Phospholipids are amphipathic. In water the hydrophilic phosphate heads associate with water while the hydrophobic fatty acid tails are excluded from it, so the molecules spontaneously arrange themselves in a double layer with heads outwards and tails inwards; no enzymes are needed.
rationales: Phospholipids are amphipathic. In water the hydrophilic phosphate heads associate with water while the hydrophobic fatty acid tails are excluded from it, so the molecules spontaneously arrange themselves in a double layer with heads outwards and tails inwards; no enzymes are needed.

A student who assumes every biological structure is built by enzymes picks this. Bilayer formation is a consequence of the hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions of the molecule and happens spontaneously in water.

A student who expects an orderly structure to be covalently bonded picks this. No covalent bonds form between phospholipids; the bilayer is held by the exclusion of the tails from water, which leaves it fluid.

A student who confuses amphipathic with amphoteric picks this. Amphipathic means having a hydrophilic and a hydrophobic region, and it is this that drives bilayer formation; no acid–base reaction with water occurs.

mcqs.q: Testosterone binds to receptors inside its target cells. How does it get through the plasma membrane to reach them?
options: It is too large to pass between the phospholipids, so it is carried through a channel protein
It is a non-polar steroid, so it dissolves in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer and diffuses across
It is a protein hormone, so it is pulled into the cell after binding to a receptor on the surface
It is enclosed in a vesicle at the cell surface and taken into the cell by endocytosis
mcqs.specStatementText: Steroids slip through the bilayer
mcqs.explain: Testosterone is a steroid, a lipid built on four fused carbon rings, and is non-polar. It dissolves in the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer and passes through by simple diffusion, which is why steroid hormones can act on receptors inside the cell.
rationales: A student who applies the rule that only small molecules cross the bilayer picks this. Polarity matters more than size here: non-polar steroids dissolve in the bilayer itself and need no channel.

Testosterone is a steroid, a lipid built on four fused carbon rings, and is non-polar. It dissolves in the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer and passes through by simple diffusion, which is why steroid hormones can act on receptors inside the cell.
A student who assumes all hormones are proteins picks this. Testosterone is a steroid lipid, not a protein; protein hormones cannot cross the bilayer, whereas steroids can.
A student who defaults to endocytosis for anything entering a cell picks this. A steroid needs no vesicle: being non-polar it diffuses straight through the hydrophobic core of the membrane.

mcqs.q: Four molecules are drawn as molecular diagrams. Which description identifies the molecule that is a steroid?
options: A single six-membered ring made up of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom
A chain of amino acids folded up into a compact globular shape
Four fused rings of carbon atoms, three with six atoms and one with five
A glycerol backbone joined to three long hydrocarbon chains
mcqs.specStatementText: Steroids slip through the bilayer
mcqs.explain: A steroid is recognized by its four fused rings sharing edges, three six-membered and one five-membered. Oestradiol and testosterone both have this structure, which is non-polar and lets them pass through the phospholipid bilayer.
rationales: A student who treats any ring as the mark of a steroid picks this. A single ring containing an oxygen atom, with carbon outside it, is the ring form of a hexose such as glucose.
A student who thinks steroid hormones are proteins picks this. A folded amino acid chain is a protein; steroids are lipids with four fused rings and no amino acids.

A steroid is recognized by its four fused rings sharing edges, three six-membered and one five-membered. Oestradiol and testosterone both have this structure, which is non-polar and lets them pass through the phospholipid bilayer.
A student who equates lipids with fats picks this, choosing the fat. This is a triglyceride; steroids are a different class of lipid with a fused-ring structure rather than fatty acid chains.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids

specStatements.text: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
Hydrolysis splits polymers back into monomers
Monosaccharides, and why glucose suits its job
Starch and glycogen store energy compactly
Cellulose: straight chains bundled into a strong wall
Glycoproteins let cells recognize each other
Lipids are defined by what they dissolve in
Triglycerides and phospholipids are built by condensation
Double bonds, melting point and where fats are stored
Adipose tissue: energy store and insulator

scopeNotes.howHonoured: The nature-of-science content is limited to the five named prefixes and to the idea that their meanings are agreed conventions. No other prefixes (mega, giga, pico) are used in any item, and the history of the SI system and the bodies that maintain it are not tested.

Phospholipids are described only as glycerol linked to two fatty acids and a phosphate group. The additional polar groups attached to the phosphate in named phospholipids (choline, serine, ethanolamine) and the names of individual phospholipids are not included, and the ester bond is named but its mechanism is not examined.

Steroids are identified only by the four fused carbon rings (three six-membered and one five-membered) that a molecular diagram shows, described in words. The functional groups that distinguish oestradiol from testosterone, the synthesis of steroids from cholesterol and the mechanism of steroid receptors are not included.
